title.zh: 卷五十三 吳書八 張嚴程闞薛傳
title.en: Volume 53: Book of Wu 8 - Biographies of Zhang, Yan, Cheng, Kan, and Xue
title.raw: 卷五十三 吳書八 張嚴程闞薛傳 Volume 53: Book of Wu 8 - Biographies of Zhang, Yan, Cheng, Kan, and Xue

sentences.zh: 張紘字子綱，廣陵人。

translations.literal: Zhang Hong, courtesy name Zigang, was a man of Guangling.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Hong, whose courtesy name was Zigang, came from Guangling.

sentences.zh: 少遊學京都，

translations.literal: In his youth he traveled to study in the capital.
translations.idiomatic: While still young he went to the capital to pursue his studies.

sentences.zh: 〈吳書曰：纮入太學，事博士韓宗，治京氏易、歐陽尚書，又於外黃從濮陽闓受《韓詩》及《禮記》、《左氏春秋》。〉

translations.literal: The Book of Wu states: Hong entered the Imperial Academy and served the erudite Han Zong, studying the Jing interpretation of the Changes and the Ouyang Documents; at Waihuang he also studied under Puyang Kai the Han Odes, the Record of Rites, and Zuo's Commentary to the Spring and Autumn.
translations.idiomatic: The Wu chronicle adds that he enrolled in the Imperial Academy under the erudite Han Zong, took up the Jing school's Book of Changes and the Ouyang recension of the Documents, and at Waihuang learned from Puyang Kai the Han Odes, the Record of Rites, and Zuo's Commentary.

sentences.zh: 還本郡，舉茂才，公府辟，皆不就，

translations.literal: He returned to his native commandery, was nominated flourishing talent, and the high offices summoned him, yet in every case he did not take office.
translations.idiomatic: Back in Guangling he earned nomination as flourishing talent and received summons from the great ministries—but he declined every appointment.

sentences.zh: 〈吳書曰：大將軍何進、太尉硃俊、司空荀爽三府辟為掾，皆稱疾不就。〉

translations.literal: The Book of Wu states: The offices of the Great General He Jin, Grand Commandant Zhu Jun, and Minister of Works Xun Shuang each summoned him as an aide, and in every case he pleaded illness and did not take office.
translations.idiomatic: The same source records that He Jin, Zhu Jun, and Xun Shuang all tried to hire him as a clerk; each time he pleaded illness and stayed home.

sentences.zh: 避難江東。

translations.literal: He fled trouble to the east of the Yangzi.
translations.idiomatic: He crossed the river to escape the turmoil in the north.

sentences.zh: 孫策創業，遂委質焉。

translations.literal: When Sun Ce was founding his enterprise, thereupon he pledged his allegiance to him.
translations.idiomatic: When Sun Ce was carving out his new lordship in the southeast, Zhang Hong entered his service at once.

sentences.zh: 表為正議校尉，

translations.literal: He was recommended for appointment as Colonel Who Discusses What Is Correct.
translations.idiomatic: Sun Ce had him recommended as Colonel of Correct Counsel.

sentences.zh: 〈吳書曰：纮與張昭並與參謀，常令一人居守，一人從征討，後呂布襲取徐州，因為之牧，不欲令纮與策從事。

translations.literal: The Book of Wu states: Hong and Zhang Zhao both joined in planning strategy; they were regularly ordered so that one remained on guard and one accompanied the campaigns. Later Lü Bu seized Xu Province in a surprise attack and thereupon became its shepherd, and because he did not wish to let Hong follow Ce in military affairs
translations.idiomatic: The Wu documents note that Hong and Zhang Zhao shared strategic counsel, with one usually left to hold the rear while the other rode with the army—until Lü Bu seized Xu Province and made himself its governor, after which Lü kept Hong from accompanying Sun Ce.

sentences.zh: 追舉茂才，移書發遣纮。

translations.literal: he then nominated Hong flourishing talent and sent a letter summoning and dispatching Hong.
translations.idiomatic: Lü Bu then nominated Hong again for flourishing talent and ordered him north with an official summons.

sentences.zh: 纮心惡布，恥為之屈。

translations.literal: Hong's heart hated Bu and was ashamed to submit to him.
translations.idiomatic: Hong despised Lü Bu and refused to humble himself to him.

sentences.zh: 策亦重惜纮，欲以自輔。

translations.literal: Ce also greatly treasured Hong and wished to use him to assist himself.
translations.idiomatic: Sun Ce prized him just as highly and wanted him at his own side.

sentences.zh: 答記不遣，曰：「海產明珠，所在為寶，楚雖有才，晉實用之。

translations.literal: He answered with a memorandum refusing to send him off, saying, "The sea yields bright pearls—wherever they are found, they are treasure; though Chu may have talent, it is Jin that employs it.
translations.idiomatic: Sun Ce wrote back refusing to release him, arguing that fine pearls are treasure wherever the sea casts them up, and that "though Chu may boast talent, it is Jin that puts it to use"—talent is not a monopoly of one region.

sentences.zh: 英偉君子，所遊見珍，何必本州哉？」〉

translations.literal: A hero among gentlemen, wherever he roams is treated as a jewel—why must he be of this province?"〉
translations.idiomatic: A true man of stature wins regard wherever he goes; he need not hail from our own commandery alone."

sentences.zh: 從討丹揚，策身臨行陳，紘諫曰：「夫主將乃籌謨之所自出，三軍之所繫命也，不宜輕脫。

translations.literal: When he followed on the campaign against Danyang, Ce personally entered the ranks of battle; Hong remonstrated, saying, "The commander is that from which plans proceed of themselves and to which the life of the three armies is tied; it is not fitting that he should lightly expose himself.
translations.idiomatic: On the Danyang campaign Hong begged Sun Ce not to lead from the front, warning that the general is the mind of the army and the army's very life—he must not throw away his person on a whim.

sentences.zh: 自敵小寇，願麾下重天授之姿，副四海之望，無令國內上下危懼。」

translations.literal: Let the enemy be petty raiders—may Your Lordship rather cherish the stature Heaven has granted you, match the hopes of all within the four seas, and not let those above and below within the state live in alarm and fear."
translations.idiomatic: Even against a petty foe, he urged, Sun Ce should guard the authority Heaven had invested in him, answer the expectations of the realm, and spare the court the terror of seeing its chief constantly in the thick of the fight."

sentences.zh: 紘建計宜出都秣陵，權從之。

translations.literal: Hong proposed a plan that the capital ought to be moved to Moling, and Quan followed it.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Hong urged Sun Quan to make Moling his capital, and Quan accepted the advice.

sentences.zh: 〈《江表傳》曰：纮謂權曰：「秣陵，楚武王所置，名為金陵。

translations.literal: The Jiang biao zhuan states: Hong said to Quan, "Moling was established by King Wu of Chu and was named Jinling.
translations.idiomatic: The Jiangbiao zhuan records Hong telling Quan that Moling had been founded by King Wu of Chu under the name Jinling.

sentences.zh: 地勢岡阜連石頭，訪問故老，雲昔秦始皇東巡會稽經此縣，望氣者云金陵地形有王者都邑之氣，故掘斷連岡，改名秣陵。

translations.literal: The terrain consists of ridges and hills linked to Stone Hill; I have questioned old residents, who say that when the First Emperor of Qin toured east to Kuaiji he passed through this county, men who read the qi said the topography of Jinling had the aura of a king's capital, and therefore he dug through the connecting ridges and changed the name to Moling.
translations.idiomatic: The ground runs in a chain of heights toward Stone City; elders say that when the First Emperor toured east his geomancers read Jinling's breath as fit for an imperial seat, so he cut the ridge-line and renamed the place Moling.

sentences.zh: 今處所具存，地有其氣，天之所命，宜為都邑。

translations.literal: The traces of the place are still present, the ground still has that qi—it is Heaven's mandate; it ought to be the capital.
translations.idiomatic: The marks of that work remain, he argued, and the site's royal aura is still Heaven's own verdict—it should be the seat of government.

sentences.zh: 」權善其議，未能從也。

translations.literal: "Quan thought well of the proposal but was not yet able to follow it.
translations.idiomatic: Quan praised the plan but did not adopt it immediately.

sentences.zh: 後劉備之東，宿於秣陵，周觀地形，亦勸權都之。

translations.literal: Later, when Liu Bei went east and lodged at Moling, he too toured the terrain and likewise urged Quan to make it his capital.
translations.idiomatic: Later Liu Bei came east, stayed at Moling, walked the ground himself, and urged Sun Quan to move the court there as well.

sentences.zh: 權曰：「智者意同。

translations.literal: Quan said, "Men of wisdom share one mind.
translations.idiomatic: Sun Quan replied, "Wise men read the land the same way."

sentences.zh: 」遂都焉。

translations.literal: "Thereupon he established the capital there.
translations.idiomatic: He then made Moling his capital.

sentences.zh: 獻帝春秋云：劉備至京，謂孫權曰：「吳去此數百里，即有警急，赴救為難，將軍無意屯京乎？

translations.literal: The Annals of Emperor Xian states: When Liu Bei reached Jing, he said to Sun Quan, "Wu is several hundred li from here; if there is sudden alarm, rushing to the rescue is hard—has the General no thought of stationing troops at Jing?
translations.idiomatic: The Annals of Emperor Xian relate that after Liu Bei arrived at the capital he asked Sun Quan whether Wu, hundreds of li away, could really reinforce the capital in a crisis, and suggested garrisoning Jing.

sentences.zh: 」權曰：「秣陵有小江百餘里，可以安大船，吾方理水軍，當移據之。

translations.literal: "Quan said, "Moling has a small river over a hundred li on which large ships can be anchored; I am just now organizing the navy and ought to move my base there.
translations.idiomatic: Quan answered that Moling's hundred-li back-channel could hold heavy warships and that his naval buildup made a move there the logical next step.

sentences.zh: 」備曰：「蕪湖近濡須，亦佳也。

translations.literal: "Bei said, "Wuhu is close to Ruxu—that is also excellent.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Bei countered that Wuhu near Ruxu would serve just as well.

sentences.zh: 」權曰：「吾欲圖徐州，宜近下也。

translations.literal: "Quan said, "I intend to strike toward Xu Province and ought to be close to the lower reaches.
translations.idiomatic: Quan replied that he planned operations against Xu Province and needed a base farther downriver.

sentences.zh: 」臣松之以為秣陵之與蕪湖，道里所校無幾，於北侵利便，亦有何異？

translations.literal: "Your servant Songzhi considers that between Moling and Wuhu the difference in road is not much, and for advantage in raiding north, wherein does one differ from the other?
translations.idiomatic: Pei Songzhi objects that Moling and Wuhu are scarcely different in marching distance for a northern offensive.

sentences.zh: 而云欲闚徐州，貪秣陵近下，非其理也。

translations.literal: Yet to say he wished to spy on Xu and for that reason greedily preferred Moling for being close to the lower reaches is not its principle.
translations.idiomatic: To argue that Quan chose Moling chiefly to keep an eye on Xu Province is strained logic.

sentences.zh: 諸書皆云劉備勸都秣陵，而此獨雲權自欲都之，又為虛錯。〉

translations.literal: All the various books state that Liu Bei urged a capital at Moling, while this alone says Quan himself wished to make it the capital—it is again a false error."〉
translations.idiomatic: Every other account credits Liu Bei with the Moling plan; only this passage says Quan acted on his own—another slip of the brush, in Pei's judgment."

sentences.zh: 令還吳迎家，道病卒。

translations.literal: He was ordered to return to Wu to welcome his family; on the road he fell ill and died.
translations.idiomatic: Ordered back to Wu to fetch his household, he took sick en route and died.

sentences.zh: 臨困，授子靖留箋曰：「自古有國有家者，咸欲修德政以比隆盛世，至於其治，多不馨香。

translations.literal: On the verge of death he handed his son Jing a parting note, saying, "From antiquity, those who had states or households all wished to cultivate virtuous government so as to rival the height of a flourishing age; as for their actual rule, most did not achieve a fragrant reputation.
translations.idiomatic: Dying, he gave his son Jing a letter lamenting how rulers since antiquity had hoped for virtuous rule worthy of a golden age yet rarely left behind an administration that smelled sweet.

sentences.zh: 非無忠臣賢佐暗於治體也，由主不勝其情，弗能用耳。

translations.literal: It is not that they lacked loyal ministers and worthy helpers who were ignorant of the body of good government; it comes from the lord being unable to master his passions and therefore not employing them.
translations.idiomatic: The fault, he insisted, was seldom for lack of loyal advisers who understood statecraft, but because sovereigns surrendered to appetite and would not heed them.

sentences.zh: 夫人情憚難而趨易，好同而惡異，與治道相反。

translations.literal: Now human feelings shrink from the difficult and hasten toward the easy, love sameness and hate difference—they oppose the way of good government.
translations.idiomatic: Human nature flees hardship for ease and conformity for dissent—the very opposite of sound rule.

sentences.zh: 《傳》曰：『從善如登，從惡如崩』，言善之難也。

translations.literal: The Tradition states: "To follow the good is like climbing a height; to follow evil is like tumbling down a bank"—it speaks of how hard the good is.
translations.idiomatic: As the Classic says, virtue is an uphill climb and vice a downhill run—the good is simply harder won.

sentences.zh: 人君承奕世之基，據自然之勢，操八柄之威，甘易同之歡，

translations.literal: The lord of men inherits foundations laid for generations, occupies a position of natural advantage, wields the majesty of the Eight Handles, and indulges in the pleasures of what is easy and what agrees with him,
translations.idiomatic: A ruler sits on ages of accumulated power, leans on inherent advantage, holds the eight levers of control described in the Zhou li, yet still craves easy consensus—

sentences.zh: 〈《周禮太宰職》曰：以八柄詔王馭群臣。

translations.literal: The Office of the Grand Steward in the Zhou li states: By means of the Eight Handles he instructs the king to regulate the host of ministers.
translations.idiomatic: the Grand Steward's chapter lists eight "handles" by which the throne steers its officials.

sentences.zh: 一曰爵，以馭其貴。

translations.literal: The first is ennoblement, by which to regulate their honor.
translations.idiomatic: First, rank and title to secure their standing.

sentences.zh: 二曰祿，以馭其富。

translations.literal: The second is salary, by which to regulate their wealth.
translations.idiomatic: Second, stipends to secure their fortune.

sentences.zh: 三曰予，以馭其幸。

translations.literal: The third is largess, by which to regulate their favor.
translations.idiomatic: Third, gifts to bind their gratitude.

sentences.zh: 四曰置，以馭其行。

translations.literal: The fourth is appointment, by which to regulate their conduct.
translations.idiomatic: Fourth, placement in office to shape their conduct.

sentences.zh: 五曰生，以馭其福。

translations.literal: The fifth is keeping alive, by which to regulate their blessing.
translations.idiomatic: Fifth, sparing life to preserve their good fortune.

sentences.zh: 六曰奪，以馭其貧。

translations.literal: The sixth is confiscation, by which to regulate their poverty.
translations.idiomatic: Sixth, stripping wealth to humble the over-rich.

sentences.zh: 七曰廢，以馭其罪。

translations.literal: The seventh is dismissal, by which to regulate their crimes.
translations.idiomatic: Seventh, removal from office to answer their guilt.

sentences.zh: 八曰誅，以馭其過。〉

translations.literal: The eighth is execution, by which to regulate their faults."〉
translations.idiomatic: Eighth, capital punishment to answer grave fault."

sentences.zh: 無假取於人；

translations.literal: He has no need to borrow anything from others;
translations.idiomatic: He fancies he owes nothing to counsel drawn from outside himself—

sentences.zh: 而忠臣挾難近之術，吐逆耳之言，其不合也，不亦宜乎！

translations.literal: yet loyal ministers embrace methods hard to draw near, speak words that grate on the ear—when they fail to fit with him, is it not fitting!
translations.idiomatic: —while loyal ministers bring awkward remedies and blunt speech; no wonder they so often fall out of step with their lord.

translations.literal: (Although)
translations.idiomatic: Even then—

sentences.zh: 則有釁，巧辯緣間，眩於小忠，戀於恩愛，賢愚雜錯，長幼失敘，其所由來，情亂之也。

translations.literal: then there are flaws; clever disputers seize openings from the gaps, they are dazzled by petty devotion and cling to feelings of kindness; worthy and foolish are jumbled, elders and juniors lose their proper order—the source from which it comes is that passion throws everything into confusion.
translations.idiomatic: —fault-finding thrives, flatterers exploit every crack, petty loyalty dazzles the ruler, private affection clouds judgment, wise and foolish are mixed, and proper order between old and young collapses; passion is always the root of the chaos.

sentences.zh: 故明君悟之，求賢如饑渴。

translations.literal: Therefore the enlightened ruler perceives this and seeks the worthy as if famished and thirsty.
translations.idiomatic: A clear-sighted ruler sees that danger and hunts talent as hungrily as a starving man seeks food.

sentences.zh: 受諫而不厭，抑情損欲，以義割恩，上無偏謬之授，下無冀之望。

translations.literal: He receives remonstrance without growing weary, suppresses passion and diminishes desire, severs favor by righteousness; above there is no partial or mistaken conferring of office, below there is no expectation of improper favor.
translations.idiomatic: He welcomes criticism without tiring, reins in appetite and affection, and lets duty cut through private ties, so that appointments above stay fair and no one below nurses vain hopes of pull.

sentences.zh: 宜加三思，含垢藏疾，以成仁覆之大。

translations.literal: You ought thrice to reflect, endure shame and harbor resentments, so as to accomplish the great canopy of benevolent oversight.
translations.idiomatic: Think thrice, bear insult and swallow grievance, and so fulfill the broad compassion expected of a true ruler.

sentences.zh: 」時年六十卒。

translations.literal: "At age sixty he died.
translations.idiomatic: He died that year at the age of sixty.

sentences.zh: 權省書流涕。

translations.literal: Quan, on reading the letter, wept.
translations.idiomatic: Sun Quan wept when he read the testament.

sentences.zh: 紘著詩賦銘誄十餘篇。

translations.literal: Hong composed odes, fu, inscriptions, and dirges—more than ten pieces.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Hong left behind more than ten pieces of verse and commemorative prose—odes, rhapsodies, inscriptions, and laments.

sentences.zh: 〈《吳書》曰：纮見柟榴枕，愛其文，為作賦。

translations.literal: The Book of Wu states: Hong saw a nanliu-wood pillow, loved its grain, and composed a fu on it.
translations.idiomatic: The Book of Wu notes that he wrote a rhapsody on a rosewood pillow whose grain charmed him.

sentences.zh: 陳琳在北見之，以示人曰：「此吾鄉里張子綱所作也。

translations.literal: Chen Lin in the north saw it and showed it to people, saying, "This is the work of Zigang from my home region.
translations.idiomatic: In the north Chen Lin showed the piece around, declaring it the work of his townsman Zhang Zigang.

sentences.zh: 」後纮見陳琳作武庫賦、應機論，與琳書深嘆美之。

translations.literal: "Later Hong saw Chen Lin's fu on the armory and his Discourse on Responding to Occasion, and wrote Lin a letter deeply sighing in praise of them.
translations.idiomatic: When Hong later read Chen's Armory Rhapsody and Discourse on Seizing the Moment, he wrote Chen a letter of unstinting admiration.

sentences.zh: 琳答曰：「自僕在河北，與天下隔，此間率少於文章，易為雄伯，故使僕受此過差之譚，非其實也。

translations.literal: Lin replied, "Since your servant has been north of the Yellow River, separated from the world, in this region literature has generally been scarce, so it is easy to stand as chief bull—therefore they have made your servant receive these excessive praises, which are not the reality.
translations.idiomatic: Chen answered deprecatingly that isolation in Hebei had left few writers to compare against, so northerners flattered him beyond his deserts.

sentences.zh: 今景興在此，足下與子佈在彼，所謂小巫見大巫，神氣盡矣。

translations.literal: Now with Jingxing here and you and Zibu over there, it is what is called the petty wizard seeing the great wizard—the spirit is entirely gone.
translations.idiomatic: "With Yu Fan here and you and Zhang Zhao there," he added, "it is the little shaman meeting the great one—every pretense of skill collapses."

sentences.zh: 」纮既好文學，又善楷篆，與孔融書，自書。

translations.literal: "Hong both loved literature and was skilled in regular script and seal script; he wrote his own letter to Kong Rong.
translations.idiomatic: Hong was not only a lover of letters but a fine calligrapher in standard and seal scripts, and he penned his own correspondence to Kong Rong.

sentences.zh: 融遺纮書曰：「前勞手筆，多篆書。

translations.literal: Rong sent Hong a letter, saying, "Before this you took trouble with your own hand, mostly in seal script.
translations.idiomatic: Kong Rong wrote back that whenever Hong's brush arrived, usually in seal characters,

sentences.zh: 每舉篇見字，欣然獨笑，如復睹其人也。」〉

translations.literal: each time I raised the piece and saw the characters, I smiled alone with joy, as if I were seeing the man again."〉
translations.idiomatic: opening the scroll felt like meeting the writer in person."

sentences.zh: 子玄，官至南郡太守、尚書。

translations.literal: His son Xuan reached the offices of Administrator of Nan Commandery and Palace Attendant.
translations.idiomatic: His son Zhang Xuan rose to governor of Nan commandery and ministerial secretary at court.

sentences.zh: 〈《江表傳》曰：玄清介有高行，而才不及纮。〉

translations.literal: The Jiang biao zhuan states: Xuan was pure, upright, and of lofty conduct, but his talent did not reach Hong's."〉
translations.idiomatic: The Jiangbiao zhuan adds that Zhang Xuan was scrupulous and high-minded, though he lacked his father's brilliance."

sentences.zh: 玄子尚，

translations.literal: Xuan's son Shang,
translations.idiomatic: Xuan was succeeded by his son Shang—

sentences.zh: 〈《江表傳》

translations.literal: The Jiang biao zhuan
translations.idiomatic: the Jiangbiao zhuan

translations.literal: (states)
translations.idiomatic: records—

sentences.zh: 稱尚有俊才。〉

translations.literal: stated that Shang had outstanding ability."〉
translations.idiomatic: —that the younger Zhang Shang possessed exceptional talent."

sentences.zh: 孫皓時為侍郎，以言語辯捷見知，擢為侍中、中書令。

translations.literal: During the time of Sun Hao he was Gentleman of the Household; because he was known for quick and fluent speech he was promoted to Palace Attendant and Palace Secretary.
translations.idiomatic: Under Sun Hao he began as a gentleman cadet, then won promotion to palace attendant and chief secretary for his ready tongue.

sentences.zh: 皓使尚鼓琴，尚對曰：「素不能。

translations.literal: Hao ordered Shang to play the zither; Shang replied, "Plainly I cannot.
translations.idiomatic: When Hao told him to play the qin, Shang answered flatly that he could not.

sentences.zh: 」敕使學之。

translations.literal: "He was commanded to learn it.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor ordered him to learn.

sentences.zh: 後宴言次說琴之精妙，尚因道「晉平公使師曠作清角，曠言吾君德薄，不足以聽之。

translations.literal: Later, during a banquet when talk turned to the fineness of the zither, Shang thereupon cited that "Duke Ping of Jin ordered Music Master Kuang to perform the Qingjiao air; Kuang said my lord's virtue was thin and not sufficient to hear it.
translations.idiomatic: Later, at a feast, talk turned to the subtleties of the instrument and Shang quoted how Duke Ping of Jin once asked blind Master Kuang for the Qingjiao tune and Kuang refused on grounds of the duke's slight virtue.

sentences.zh: 」皓意謂尚以斯喻己，不悅。

translations.literal: "Hao's intention was that Shang was using this story to liken himself to Hao, and he was displeased.
translations.idiomatic: Hao assumed Shang was likening him to Duke Ping and took offense.

sentences.zh: 後積他事下獄，皆追此為詰，

translations.literal: Later, when other matters accumulated and he was cast into prison, all pursued this as the point of interrogation,
translations.idiomatic: When Shang later fell into jail on accumulated charges, interrogators kept circling back to that banquet remark.

sentences.zh: 〈環氏《吳紀》曰：皓嘗問：「詩云『汎彼栢舟』，惟栢中舟乎？

translations.literal: Huan's Wu ji states: Hao once asked, "The Odes say 'Float that cypress boat'—does it mean only cypress makes boats fit?
translations.idiomatic: Huan Kai's Wu ji records Hao quizzing him whether the Classic's "cypress boat" meant only cypress wood would do.

sentences.zh: 」尚對曰：「詩言『檜楫松舟』，則松亦中舟也。

translations.literal: "Shang replied, "The ode also speaks of 'oak oars and pine boat,' so pine also makes boats fit for the river.
translations.idiomatic: Shang answered with another line—oak oars and pine hulls—to show more than cypress was meant.

sentences.zh: 」又問：「鳥之大者惟鶴，小者惟雀乎？

translations.literal: "He also asked, "Among birds the great ones are only the crane; are the small ones only the sparrow?
translations.idiomatic: Hao pressed him on whether the crane was uniquely the largest bird and the sparrow the smallest.

sentences.zh: 」尚對曰：「大者有禿鶖，小者有鷦鷯。

translations.literal: "Shang replied, "There are greater birds such as the condor, and smaller ones such as the wren.
translations.idiomatic: Shang cited birds far larger than cranes and wren-tits smaller than sparrows.

sentences.zh: 」皓性忌勝己，而尚談論每出其表，積以致恨。

translations.literal: "Hao by nature hated anyone who surpassed himself, yet Shang's discussions constantly rose above his table, and accumulated until it became hatred.
translations.idiomatic: Because Hao could not bear anyone to outshine him while Shang habitually one-upped him in debate, resentment piled up.

sentences.zh: 後問：「孤飲酒以方誰？

translations.literal: Later he asked, "With whom do you compare my drinking?
translations.idiomatic: Later Hao demanded to know whose drinking habit Shang thought matched his own.

sentences.zh: 」尚對曰：「陛下有百觚之量。

translations.literal: "Shang replied, "Your Majesty has the capacity of a hundred goblets.
translations.idiomatic: Shang answered that the emperor could put away a hundred cups.

sentences.zh: 」皓云：「尚知孔丘之不王，而以孤方之！

translations.literal: "Hao said, "Shang knows that Confucius never became king, yet compares me to him!
translations.idiomatic: Hao exploded that Shang had compared him to Confucius—the sage who never gained a throne.

sentences.zh: 」因此發怒收尚。

translations.literal: "Thereupon in anger he seized Shang.
translations.idiomatic: On that pretext Hao had him arrested.

sentences.zh: 尚書岑昬率公卿已下百餘人，詣宮叩頭請，尚罪得減死。〉

translations.literal: Minister of the Secretariat Cen Hun led the Excellencies and below, more than a hundred men, to the palace to kowtow and plead; Shang's crime was mitigated to commutation of death."〉
translations.idiomatic: Cen Hun led more than a hundred officials from the Three Excellencies down in a gate vigil that commuted Shang's sentence from death."

sentences.zh: 送建安作船。

translations.literal: He was sent to Jian'an to build ships.
translations.idiomatic: He was banished to Jian'an to labor in the shipyards.

sentences.zh: 久之，又就加誅。

translations.literal: After a long time, he was again subjected to execution.
translations.idiomatic: Months later further charges brought his execution.

sentences.zh: 初，紘同郡秦松字文表，陳端字子正，並與紘見待於孫策，參與謀謨。

translations.literal: At the outset, Hong's fellow commandery-men Qin Song, courtesy name Wenbiao, and Chen Duan, courtesy name Zizheng, were both treated with favor by Sun Ce and joined in planning strategy.
translations.idiomatic: Earlier, Hong's countrymen Qin Song (Wenbiao) and Chen Duan (Zizheng) had stood with him in Sun Ce's favor and shared in his strategic counsel.

sentences.zh: 各早卒。

translations.literal: Both died early.
translations.idiomatic: Both men died young.

sentences.zh: 嚴畯字曼才，彭城人也。

translations.literal: Yan Jun, courtesy name Mancai, was a man of Pengcheng.
translations.idiomatic: Yan Jun, courtesy name Mancai, came from Pengcheng.

sentences.zh: 少耽學，善《詩》、《書》、三《禮》，又好《說文》。

translations.literal: In his youth he loved study and was good at the Odes, the Documents, and the three Ritual classics; he also loved the Shuowen.
translations.idiomatic: Devoted to learning from boyhood, he mastered the Odes, the Documents, and the three ritual texts, and loved Xu Shen's Shuowen dictionary as well.

sentences.zh: 避亂江東，與諸葛瑾、步騭齊名友善。

translations.literal: He fled turmoil to the east of the Yangzi and with Zhuge Jin and Bu Zhi was equally famed and on friendly terms.
translations.idiomatic: He crossed south with the refugees, forming with Zhuge Jin and Bu Zhi the region's best-known trio of scholars.

sentences.zh: 性質直純厚，其於人物，忠告善道，志存補益。

translations.literal: His nature was honest, blunt, simple, and thick; toward others in human matters he advised in good faith and urged the good way, his intent being to help.
translations.idiomatic: Plainspoken, warm, and earnest, he gave friends candid counsel in the hope of doing genuine good.

sentences.zh: 張昭進之於孫權，權以為騎都尉、從事中郎。

translations.literal: Zhang Zhao presented him to Sun Quan, and Quan appointed him Commandant of Cavalry and Consultant in the Bureau of Documents.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Zhao introduced him to Sun Quan, who named him cavalry commandant and secretary-adviser.

sentences.zh: 及橫江將軍魯肅卒，權以畯代肅，督兵萬人，鎮據陸口。

translations.literal: When General Who Crosses the River Lu Su died, Quan had Jun replace Su, commanding ten thousand troops and holding Lukou.
translations.idiomatic: When Lu Su died, Quan tried to put Yan Jun in his place at Lukou with a ten-thousand-man army.

sentences.zh: 眾人咸為畯喜。

translations.literal: The host of men all rejoiced for Jun.
translations.idiomatic: The court congratulated him on the promotion.

sentences.zh: 畯前後固辭：「樸素書生，不閒軍事，非才而據，咎悔必至。

translations.literal: Jun firmly declined before and after, saying, "I am a rustic scholar, not practiced in military affairs; if I take a post beyond my ability, remorse is bound to follow.
translations.idiomatic: Yan Jun refused again and again, protesting that he was only a bookish man who knew nothing of war and would court disaster if foisted on command.

sentences.zh: 」發言慷慨，至於流涕，

translations.literal: "He spoke with vehement earnestness until the tears flowed,
translations.idiomatic: He argued himself hoarse to the point of tears—

sentences.zh: 〈志林曰：權又試畯騎，上馬墮鞍。〉

translations.literal: The Zhi lin states: Quan also put Jun to a horseback trial, and Jun fell from the saddle."〉
translations.idiomatic: —and the Zhi lin adds that when Quan made him mount a horse to prove himself, he tumbled straight off the saddle."

sentences.zh: 權乃聽焉，世嘉其能以實讓。

translations.literal: Quan thereupon assented to it; the age praised his ability to yield office in truth.
translations.idiomatic: Sun Quan yielded to his pleas, and later generations honored him for declining a post he could not honestly fill.

sentences.zh: 權為吳王，及稱尊號，畯嘗為衛尉，使至蜀，蜀相諸葛亮深善之。

translations.literal: When Quan was King of Wu and when he assumed the imperial title, Jun had served as Commandant of the Guards and was sent on mission to Shu; Prime Minister Zhuge Liang of Shu thought very highly of him.
translations.idiomatic: After Quan became King of Wu and then emperor, Yan Jun served as commandant of the guards and envoy to Shu, where Zhuge Liang formed the highest opinion of him.

sentences.zh: 不畜祿賜，皆散之親戚知故，家常不充。

translations.literal: He did not hoard stipends and imperial gifts, but scattered them among kin and old acquaintances; his household was often not adequately supplied.
translations.idiomatic: He never stockpiled salary or largesse, passing every coin to relatives and old friends until his own house often ran short.

sentences.zh: 廣陵劉穎與畯有舊，穎精學家巷，權聞徵之，以疾不就。

translations.literal: Liu Ying of Guangling was old friends with Jun; Ying was a scholar skilled in learning in his lane; when Quan heard of him he summoned him, but on grounds of illness he did not take office.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Ying of Guangling, Yan Jun’s longtime friend, was a recluse scholar of deep learning; when Sun Quan summoned him he pleaded sickness and stayed away.

sentences.zh: 其弟略為零陵太守，卒官，穎往赴喪，權知其詐病，急驛收錄。

translations.literal: His younger brother Lüe was Administrator of Lingling; he died in office, and Ying went to attend the funeral. Quan knew he had feigned illness and urgently sent post-riders to seize and imprison him.
translations.idiomatic: When Liu Ying’s brother Liu Lüe died in office as governor of Lingling, Liu Ying traveled south for the funeral—whereupon Quan, seeing through his old excuse, had him arrested by express courier.

sentences.zh: 畯亦馳語穎，使還謝權。

translations.literal: Jun also sent a galloping message to Ying, telling him to return and apologize to Quan.
translations.idiomatic: Yan Jun raced word to Liu Ying urging him to hurry back and make his peace with the throne.

sentences.zh: 權怒廢畯，而穎得免罪。

translations.literal: Quan angrily dismissed Jun, but Ying was able to escape punishment.
translations.idiomatic: Quan stripped Yan Jun of office in his fury, yet spared Liu Ying once the man presented himself.

sentences.zh: 久之，以畯為尚書令，後卒。

translations.literal: After a long interval he appointed Jun Director of the Masters of Writing; later Jun died.
translations.idiomatic: Years later Yan Jun was recalled as director of the secretariat; he died in that role.

sentences.zh: 〈吳書曰：晙時年七十八，二子凱、爽。

translations.literal: The Book of Wu states: Jun was then seventy-eight sui; he had two sons, Kai and Shuang.
translations.idiomatic: The Book of Wu records that he was seventy-eight at his death and left two sons, Kai and Shuang.

sentences.zh: 凱官至昇平少府。〉

translations.literal: Kai rose to the office of Junior Guardian of Shengping.〉
translations.idiomatic: Yan Kai rose to junior guardian of the Shengping workshops.〉

sentences.zh: 畯著《孝經傳》、《潮水論》，又與裴玄、張承論管仲、季路。

translations.literal: Jun composed a Commentary on the Classic of Filial Piety, a Discourse on Tidal Waters, and also debated with Pei Xuan and Zhang Cheng concerning Guan Zhong and Jilu.
translations.idiomatic: Yan Jun wrote a commentary on the Classic of Filial Piety, a treatise on tides, and exchanged essays with Pei Xuan and Zhang Cheng on Guan Zhong and Zilu.

sentences.zh: 皆傳於世。

translations.literal: All circulated in the world.
translations.idiomatic: All of these works survived in circulation.

sentences.zh: 玄字彥黃，下邳人也，亦有學行，官至太中大夫。

translations.literal: Xuan, courtesy name Yanhuang, was a man of Xiapi; he too had learning and conduct, and rose to Palace Counselor.
translations.idiomatic: Pei Xuan, courtesy Yanhuang, came from Xiapi; he was another scholar of substance who reached the post of palace counselor.

sentences.zh: 問子欽齊桓、晉文、夷、惠四人優劣，欽答所見，與玄相反覆，各有文理。

translations.literal: He asked his son Qin about the comparative merit of the four—Duke Huan of Qi, Duke Wen of Jin, Boyi, and Hui of Liu-Xia; Qin answered with what he had seen, going back and forth with Xuan, each side having its pattern of argument.
translations.idiomatic: Pei Xuan once pressed his son Pei Qin to rank Duke Huan, Duke Wen, Boyi, and Liu Xiahui; father and son argued the point at length, each line of reasoning tightly woven.

sentences.zh: 欽與太子登遊處，登稱其翰採。

translations.literal: Qin associated in travel with Heir Deng, who praised the polish of Qin’s brush.
translations.idiomatic: Pei Qin kept company with the heir apparent Deng, who admired the brilliance of his writing.

sentences.zh: 程秉字德樞，汝南南頓人也。

translations.literal: Cheng Bing, courtesy name Deshu, was a man of Nandun in Runan.
translations.idiomatic: Cheng Bing, courtesy Deshu, was a native of Nandun in Runan.

sentences.zh: 逮事鄭玄，後避亂交州，與劉熙考論大義，遂博通五經。

translations.literal: He had attended on Zheng Xuan; later he fled turmoil to Jiaozhou, where with Liu Xi he examined the great meanings of the classics, and thereby came to broad mastery of the Five Classics.
translations.idiomatic: He studied under Zheng Xuan, then fled south to Jiaozhou, where debates with Liu Xi on the great texts gave him command of the entire Five Classics corpus.

sentences.zh: 士燮命為長史。

translations.literal: Shi Xie appointed him Chief Clerk.
translations.idiomatic: Shi Xie named him chief clerk of his staff.

sentences.zh: 權聞其名儒，以禮徵，秉既到，拜太子太傅。

translations.literal: On hearing of him as a famous scholar, Quan summoned him with ritual courtesies; when Bing arrived he was appointed Grand Tutor to the Heir.
translations.idiomatic: Sun Quan, hearing his reputation, summoned him with full ceremony and, on his arrival, made him grand tutor to the crown prince.

sentences.zh: 黃武四年，權為太子登娉周瑜女，秉守太常，迎妃於吳，權親幸秉船，深見優禮。

translations.literal: In the fourth year of Huangwu, when Quan had the Heir Deng take in marriage the daughter of Zhou Yu, Bing as Guardian of the Heir of State went to Wu to welcome the consort; Quan personally visited Bing’s ship and showed him deep favor and courtesy.
translations.idiomatic: In Huangwu 4, when the heir took Lady Zhou’s daughter as his bride, Cheng Bing—as minister of the heir’s household—escorted her from Wu while Sun Quan himself boarded his boat to honor him.

sentences.zh: 既還，秉從容進說登曰：「婚姻人倫之始，王教之基，是以聖王重之，所以率先眾庶，風化天下，故《詩》美《關睢》，以為稱首。

translations.literal: When they had returned, Bing calmly advanced counsel to Deng, saying, “Marriage is the beginning of human relations, the foundation of royal teaching; therefore the sage kings have held it weighty, using it to lead the common multitude first and transform customs throughout the world—for which reason the Odes praise “Guan ju” and take it as the first piece.
translations.idiomatic: After the wedding Cheng Bing quietly lectured the heir: marriage begins the moral order that kingship rests on, which is why sage-kings treated it as the lever that moves the people—hence the Odes open with “Guan ju.”

sentences.zh: 願太子尊禮教於閨房，存《周南》之所詠，則道化隆於上，頌聲作於下矣。

translations.literal: I hope the Heir will honor ritual instruction within the women’s quarters and keep in mind what the “Zhou nan” celebrates; then the transformation of the Way will flourish above and songs of praise will arise below.
translations.idiomatic: He urged the prince to let ritual govern the inner chambers and to live up to the virtues hymned in the “Zhou nan,” so that reform would start at court and praise spread through the realm.

sentences.zh: 」登笑曰：「將順其美，匡救其惡，誠所賴於傅君也。

translations.literal: Deng smiled and said, “To follow what is good in others and remedy what is evil is indeed what I depend on from the Gentleman my Tutor.”
translations.idiomatic: The heir smiled and answered, “Then I shall rely on my tutor both to encourage what is right and to check what goes wrong.”

sentences.zh: 」病卒官。

translations.literal: He died of illness in office.
translations.idiomatic: Cheng Bing died of illness while still in office.

sentences.zh: 著《周易摘》、《尚書駁》、《論語弼》，凡三萬餘言。

translations.literal: He wrote Extracts from the Zhou yi, Rebuttals on the Documents, and Aids to the Analects—in all more than thirty thousand characters.
translations.idiomatic: His published scholarship—Selections from the Changes, critiques of the Documents, and glosses on the Analects—ran to over thirty thousand graphs.

sentences.zh: 秉為傅時，率更令河南徵崇亦篤學立行云。

translations.literal: When Bing was Grand Tutor, the Director for Palace Gate Times, Zheng Chong of Henan, was also devoted to learning and of established conduct, it is said.
translations.idiomatic: While Cheng Bing tutored the heir, Zheng Chong of Henan—director of the office that kept palace gate hours—was another scholar noted for learning and upright living.

sentences.zh: 〈吳錄曰：崇字子和，治《易》、《春秋左氏傳》，兼善內術。

translations.literal: The Wu lu states: Chong, courtesy name Zihe, studied the Changes and Zuo’s Commentary to the Spring and Autumn, and was also skilled in inner techniques.
translations.idiomatic: The Wu lu records that Zheng Chong, courtesy Zihe, mastered the Changes and Zuo’s Commentary and dabbled in esoteric arts as well.

sentences.zh: 本姓李，遭亂更姓，遂隱於會稽，躬耕以求其志。

translations.literal: His original surname had been Li; encountering turmoil he changed his surname, and thereupon went into hiding in Kuaiji, personally plowing fields to seek his aim.
translations.idiomatic: Born a Li, he adopted a new surname during the wars and withdrew to Kuaiji, supporting himself by the plow while he pursued his studies.

sentences.zh: 好尚者從學，所教不過數人輒止，欲令其業必有成也。

translations.literal: Those who admired him came to study; he taught no more than a few persons at a time and then stopped, wishing that their work should necessarily succeed.
translations.idiomatic: Admirers sought him as a teacher, but he took only a handful of pupils at a time, stopping enrollment until each had truly mastered his lesson.

sentences.zh: 所交結如丞相步騭等，咸親焉。

translations.literal: Those with whom he formed ties, such as Chancellor Bu Zhi, all treated him with intimacy.
translations.idiomatic: Men like Chancellor Bu Zhi, who counted him a friend, treated him almost as family.

sentences.zh: 嚴畯薦崇行足以厲俗，學足以為師。

translations.literal: Yan Jun recommended Chong, saying his conduct was sufficient to admonish custom and his learning sufficient to serve as teacher.
translations.idiomatic: Yan Jun memorialized that Zheng Chong’s character could reform local morals and his erudition qualified him to instruct the heir.

sentences.zh: 初見太子登，以疾賜不拜。

translations.literal: On his first meeting with Heir Deng, on account of illness he was granted permission not to bow.
translations.idiomatic: At his first audience with the crown prince he was excused from full prostration on grounds of ill health.

sentences.zh: 東宮官僚皆從諮詢。

translations.literal: All the officials of the Eastern Palace followed him for consultation.
translations.idiomatic: Every member of the heir’s household staff came to him for advice.

sentences.zh: 太子數訪以異聞。

translations.literal: The Heir repeatedly visited him for unusual lore.
translations.idiomatic: The prince often dropped in to draw out his store of curious learning.

sentences.zh: 年七十而卒。〉

translations.literal: At seventy he died.〉
translations.idiomatic: He died at the age of seventy.〉

sentences.zh: 薛綜字敬文，沛郡​​竹邑人也。

translations.literal: Xue Zong, courtesy name Jingwen, was a man of Zhuyi in Pei commandery.
translations.idiomatic: Xue Zong, courtesy Jingwen, hailed from Zhuyi county in Pei commandery.

sentences.zh: 〈吳錄曰：其先齊孟嘗君封於薛。

translations.literal: The Wu lu states: His ancestors were enfeoffed at Xue when Lord Mengchang of Qi received that domain.
translations.idiomatic: The Wu lu traces the clan to the fief of Xue granted to Lord Mengchang of Qi.

sentences.zh: 秦滅六國，而失其祀，子孫分散。

translations.literal: When Qin extinguished the six states they lost their sacrifices, and descendants scattered.
translations.idiomatic: When Qin swallowed the rival kingdoms the house lost its ancestral cult, and the clan scattered.

sentences.zh: 漢祖定天下，過齊，求孟嘗後，得其孫陵、國二人，欲復其封。

translations.literal: When the Han founder settled the empire, passing through Qi he sought descendants of Lord Mengchang, found his grandsons Ling and Guo, and wished to restore their fief.
translations.idiomatic: The Han founder, marching through Qi, hunted up Lord Mengchang’s surviving grandsons Ling and Guo and meant to restore their title.

sentences.zh: 陵、國兄弟相推，莫適受，乃去之竹邑，因家焉，故遂氏薛。

translations.literal: The brothers Ling and Guo deferred to each other, neither being willing to accept; so they departed to Zhuyi and settled their family there, whereupon they took the surname Xue.
translations.idiomatic: The two brothers each refused the honor, withdrew to Zhuyi, and adopted the place-name Xue as their new surname.

sentences.zh: 自國至綜，世典州郡，為著姓。

translations.literal: From Guo down to Zong, for generations they held office in provinces and commanderies and were a prominent clan.
translations.idiomatic: From Xue Guo to Xue Zong every generation held provincial posts, making them one of the great houses of the southeast.

sentences.zh: 綜少明經，善屬文，有秀才。〉

translations.literal: Zong in his youth understood the classics and was good at composing wen; he had flourishing talent.〉
translations.idiomatic: Xue Zong mastered the classics young, wrote polished prose, and earned nomination as flourishing talent.〉

sentences.zh: 少依族人避地交州，從劉熙學。

translations.literal: In his youth he relied on a clansman to flee to the territory of Jiaozhou and studied under Liu Xi.
translations.idiomatic: As a boy he followed a kinsman into refuge in the far south and read under Liu Xi.

sentences.zh: 士燮既附孫權，召綜為五官中郎

translations.literal: After Shi Xie had submitted to Sun Quan, he summoned Zong as Commandant of the Gentlemen of the Household
translations.idiomatic: Once Shi Xie acknowledged Sun Quan’s overlordship he appointed Xue Zong captain of the household gentlemen

translations.literal: (general)
translations.idiomatic: (the title included the rank of general)

sentences.zh: ，除合浦、交阯太守。

translations.literal: , and appointed him Administrator of Hepu and Jiaozhi.
translations.idiomatic: and then named him governor of Hepu and Jiaozhi in succession.

sentences.zh: 時交土始開，刺史呂岱率師討伐，綜與俱行，越海南征，及到九真。

translations.literal: At that time the territory of Jiao was just being opened; Inspector Lü Dai led troops on campaign to subdue it; Zong accompanied him, crossed the sea on a southern expedition, and reached Jiuzhen.
translations.idiomatic: While the southern frontier was still being pacified, Xue Zong sailed with Inspector Lü Dai’s expeditionary force as far as Jiuzhen.

sentences.zh: 事畢還都，守遏者僕射。

translations.literal: When the affair was finished he returned to the capital and was appointed Supervisor of the Gatekeepers, serving as Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
translations.idiomatic: After the campaign he came back to court as supervisor of the palace gate corps and vice director of the secretariat.

sentences.zh: 西使張奉於權前列尚書闞澤姓名以嘲澤，澤不能答。

translations.literal: When the western envoy Zhang Feng before Quan listed the name of Palace Writer Kan Ze in order to mock Ze, Ze could not answer.
translations.idiomatic: At a state banquet the Shu envoy Zhang Feng punned viciously on Palace Writer Kan Ze’s name until Ze was speechless.

sentences.zh: 綜下行酒，因勸酒曰：「蜀者何也？

translations.literal: Zong went down the ranks offering wine, and taking the opportunity to urge wine he said, “As for Shu (蜀), what is it?
translations.idiomatic: Xue Zong, moving along the line with the wine ewer, stopped at Zhang Feng and asked, “Tell me—what is this ‘Shu’ of yours?”

sentences.zh: 有犬為獨，無犬為蜀，橫目苟身，蟲入其腹。」

translations.literal: With the “dog” radical it becomes “alone”; without the “dog” it is “Shu”; horizontal eyes and a hooked body—with a “worm” inside its belly.”
translations.idiomatic: He delivered the old character riddle: add the dog radical and the graph means “isolation”; strip it away and you have “Shu”—a creature with sidelong eyes, a bent torso, and a crawling thing in its gut.”

sentences.zh: 〈臣松之見諸書本「苟身」或作「句身」，以為既云「橫目」，則宜曰：「句身」。〉

translations.literal: Your servant Songzhi has seen in various book versions “gou body” or written as “ju body”; considering that since it already says “horizontal eyes,” it ought to read “ju body.”〉
translations.idiomatic: Pei Songzhi notes that manuscript copies of the riddle variously write the third phrase as *gou shen* or *ju shen*; since the couplet already speaks of “sideways eyes,” he judges *ju shen* the reading that preserves the pun.〉

sentences.zh: 奉曰：「不當復列君吳邪？

translations.literal: Feng said, “Ought I not again to set forth your Wu?”
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Feng shot back, “Shall I dissect the character ‘Wu’ for you next?”

sentences.zh: 」綜應聲曰：「無口為天，有口為吳，君臨萬邦，天子之都。

translations.literal: Zong answered on the spot: “Without a mouth it is ‘heaven’; with a mouth it is ‘Wu’; a lord overlooking ten thousand domains—the capital of the Son of Heaven.”
translations.idiomatic: Xue Zong answered instantly: “Remove the mouth and you read ‘heaven’; add the mouth and you read ‘Wu’—the ruler of myriad domains, the very seat of the Son of Heaven.”

sentences.zh: 」於是眾坐喜笑，而奉無以對。

translations.literal: Thereupon the whole assembly laughed with pleasure, while Feng had nothing to answer.
translations.idiomatic: The hall roared with laughter while Zhang Feng could find no reply.

sentences.zh: 其樞機敏捷，皆此類也。

translations.literal: The nimbleness of his pivot and trigger was all of this sort.
translations.idiomatic: His wit was always as quick and sure as that.

sentences.zh: 〈《江表傳》曰：費禕聘於吳，陛見，公卿待臣皆在坐。

translations.literal: The Jiang biao zhuan states: When Fei Yi was on a mission of courtesy to Wu, he ascended the steps for audience, and the Excellencies and ministers awaiting their lord were all seated.
translations.idiomatic: The Jiangbiao zhuan tells how Fei Yi of Shu, on embassy to Wu, mounted the dais with the full Wu court in attendance.

sentences.zh: 酒酣，禕與諸葛恪相對嘲難，言及吳、蜀。

translations.literal: When the wine was merry, Yi and Zhuge Ke faced each other in banter and challenge, talk coming to Wu and Shu.
translations.idiomatic: Late in the feast Fei Yi and Zhuge Ke traded barbed compliments about their two states.

sentences.zh: 禕問曰：「蜀字云何？

translations.literal: Yi asked, “As for the character Shu, how do you explain it?”
translations.idiomatic: Fei Yi opened with, “How would you parse the graph for ‘Shu’?”

sentences.zh: 」恪曰：「有水者濁，無水者蜀。

translations.literal: Ke said, “Where there is the water radical it is ‘turbid’; where there is no water it is ‘Shu.’
translations.idiomatic: Ke answered, “Splash it with water and you get the character for ‘murky’; dry it out and you are left with ‘Shu.’”

sentences.zh: 橫目苟身，蟲入其腹。

translations.literal: Horizontal eyes and a hooked body; a worm enters its belly.
translations.idiomatic: Same punch line as before: slanted eyes, a crooked carcass, and a bug in the belly.”

sentences.zh: 」禕復問：「吳字云何？

translations.literal: Yi asked again, “As for the character Wu, how do you explain it?”
translations.idiomatic: Fei pressed him: “And the graph for ‘Wu’?”

sentences.zh: 」恪曰：「無口者天，有口者吳，下臨滄海，天子帝都。

translations.literal: Ke said, “Without a mouth is heaven; with a mouth is Wu; below lies the vast sea—the imperial capital of the Son of Heaven.”
translations.idiomatic: Ke replied, “Lose the mouth and you read ‘heaven’; add it back and you read ‘Wu’—the realm that fronts on the boundless sea, the Son of Heaven’s own capital.”

sentences.zh: 」與本傳不同。〉

translations.literal: This differs from the main tradition.〉
translations.idiomatic: The wording differs slightly from the version preserved in this biography.〉

sentences.zh: 呂岱從交州召出，綜懼繼岱者非其人，上疏曰：

translations.literal: When Lü Dai was summoned out from Jiaozhou, Zong feared that whoever succeeded Dai might not be the right man, and submitted a memorial saying:
translations.idiomatic: When Lü Dai was recalled from the south, Xue Zong feared a bad successor and drafted a long memorial that began:

sentences.zh: 昔帝舜南巡，卒於蒼梧。

translations.literal: Formerly Emperor Shun toured to the south and died at Cangwu.
translations.idiomatic: Ancient Shun toured the south and died at Cangwu.

sentences.zh: 泰置桂林、南海、象郡，然則四國之內屬也，有自來矣。

translations.literal: The Qin established Guilin, Nanhai, and Xiang commanderies—thus within that southern belt they had been interior subjects from of old.
translations.idiomatic: The Qin organized Guilin, Nanhai, and Xiang commanderies, so that southern belt has owed allegiance to the center since high antiquity.

sentences.zh: 趙佗起番禺，懷服百越之君，珠宮之南是也。

translations.literal: Zhao Tuo arose at Panyu and brought submission from the lords of the Baiyue; south of the pearl palace is this region.
translations.idiomatic: Zhao Tuo built his power at Panyu and cowed the Yue chieftains; the country beyond the Pearl River begins there.

sentences.zh: 漢武帝誅呂嘉，開九郡，設交阯刺史以鎮監之。

translations.literal: Emperor Wu of the Han executed Lü Jia, opened nine commanderies, and set an Inspector of Jiaozhi to garrison and supervise them.
translations.idiomatic: Han Wudi crushed Lü Jia, carved nine commanderies from the land, and posted an inspector to watch over them.

sentences.zh: 山川長遠，習俗不齊，言語同異，重譯乃通。

translations.literal: Mountains and rivers extend far; customs do not match; speech is not uniform, and only through repeated interpretation can communication be achieved.
translations.idiomatic: Rugged terrain and alien tongues mean everything must pass through chains of interpreters.

sentences.zh: 民如禽獸，長幼無別，椎結徒跣，貫頭左衽，長吏之設，雖有若無。

translations.literal: The people were like birds and beasts; elder and younger had no distinctions; they wore topknots and went barefoot, pierced the forehead and draped the garment to the left; though magistrates were set up, it was as if there were none.
translations.idiomatic: The natives once lived almost like animals—no respect for age, topknots and bare feet, tattooed foreheads and left-lapped robes—so that even when the Han posted magistrates they barely registered.

sentences.zh: 自斯以來，頗徙中國罪人雜居其間，稍使學書，粗知言語，使驛往來，觀見禮化。

translations.literal: Since that time criminals from the central lands have gradually been moved to dwell among them in mixture, somewhat made to learn writing and roughly to know speech; envoys by post went back and forth so that they might observe ritual transformation.
translations.idiomatic: Later exiles from the interior were settled among them, taught a little script and speech, and linked by courier routes to court culture.

sentences.zh: 及後錫光為交阯，任延為九真太守，乃教其耕梨，使之冠履；

translations.literal: Later when Xi Guang became governor of Jiaozhi and Ren Yan became administrator of Jiuzhen, they taught them plowing with oxen, made them wear caps and shoes;
translations.idiomatic: Governors such as Xi Guang in Jiaozhi and Ren Yan in Jiuzhen introduced plow oxen, hats, and shoes.

sentences.zh: 為設媒官，始知聘娶；

translations.literal: they established matchmaker offices for them so that they first knew betrothal and marriage;
translations.idiomatic: They set up marriage brokers so that weddings followed ritual rather than impulse.

sentences.zh: 建立學校，導之經義。

translations.literal: they founded schools and guided them in the classics and meaning.
translations.idiomatic: They opened schools and drilled the people in the classics.

sentences.zh: 由此已降，四百餘年，頗有似類。

translations.literal: From then down, more than four hundred years, there have been those somewhat similar.
translations.idiomatic: For the four centuries since, something like civilization has taken root.

sentences.zh: 自臣昔客始至之時，珠崖除州縣嫁娶，皆須八月引戶，人民集會之時，男女自相可適，乃為夫妻，父母不能止。

translations.literal: From the time when I, your minister, first arrived as a client, in Zhuya—aside from commandery and county marriage regulations—all required drawing up the household registry in the eighth month, at the time when the people assembled; men and women who mutually approved of each other then became husband and wife, and parents could not stop them.
translations.idiomatic: When I first reached the coast I found that in Zhuya, outside the few registered county marriages, every household had to file rosters in the eighth month; at the festival fair young people paired off with whomever they chose, and families could not interfere.

sentences.zh: 交阯糜泠、九真都龐二縣，皆兄死弟妻其嫂，世以此為俗，長吏恣聽，不能禁制。

translations.literal: In Miling of Jiaozhi and Dulang of Jiuzhen—two counties—when an elder brother died the younger brother took his widow as wife; generation after generation they took this as custom, and magistrates indulgently listened, unable to forbid it.
translations.idiomatic: In Miling and Dulang counties a younger brother inherited his elder brother’s widow by custom, and weak officials simply looked the other way.

sentences.zh: 日郡男女夥體，不以為羞。

translations.literal: In this commandery men and women mingled bodies in groups and did not regard it as shameful.
translations.idiomatic: In that commandery men and women mingled naked in public without a blush.

sentences.zh: 由此言之，可謂蟲豸，有靦面目耳。

translations.literal: Judging from this, they may be called worms and reptiles who yet have the face to look at others.
translations.idiomatic: By central standards they behaved like beasts—yet they still possessed human faces.

sentences.zh: 然而土廣人眾，阻險毒害，易以為亂，難使從治。

translations.literal: Yet the land is broad and the people numerous, treacherous and poisonous with obstacles, easy to stir into disorder and hard to bring to order.
translations.idiomatic: The region is vast, the population large, the jungles venomous and the paths treacherous—easy to revolt and hard to govern.

sentences.zh: 縣官羈縻，示令威服，田戶之租賦，裁取供辦，貴致遠珍名珠、香藥、象牙、犀角、玳瑁、珊瑚、琉璃、鸚鵡、翡翠、孔雀、奇物，充備寶玩，不必仰其賦入，以益中國也。

translations.literal: The county command treats them loosely, displaying authority only to make them submit in awe; the rent and tax from field households—take only enough to meet needs—the prize is to secure rare treasures from afar, famous pearls, aromatics, ivory, rhinoceros horn, tortoise shell, coral, colored glass, parrots, kingfisher feathers, peacocks, curious goods, to fill the treasury of playthings; one need not rely on their grain revenue to enrich the central lands.
translations.idiomatic: Imperial policy therefore governs them lightly—enough awe to keep the peace, modest land taxes, while the real profit lies in pearls, incense, ivory, horn, tortoiseshell, coral, glass, parrots, kingfisher plumes, peacocks, and other curios for the palace workshops rather than in squeezing the fields for grain.

sentences.zh: 然在九甸之外，長吏之選，類不精核。

translations.literal: Yet lying outside the nine circuits, the selection of magistrates has generally not been meticulous.
translations.idiomatic: Because the region lies beyond the Nine Provinces, appointments there have seldom been vetted with care.

sentences.zh: 漢時法寬，多自放恣，故數反違法。

translations.literal: In Han times the law was lax, and many acted on their own inclinations, therefore they repeatedly rebelled and broke the law.
translations.idiomatic: Under the lax Han code many governors ran wild, which is why the south rose again and again.

sentences.zh: 珠崖之廢，起於長吏睹其好發，髡取為髲。

translations.literal: The abolition of Zhuya began when a magistrate saw good hair on the people, shaved it off, and took it for hairpieces.
translations.idiomatic: Zhuya was struck from the rolls after an official shaved women’s hair to sell as wigs—an outrage that sparked revolt.

sentences.zh: 及臣所見，南海黃蓋為日南太守，下車以供設不豐，撾殺主薄，仍見驅逐。

translations.literal: Further, as I have witnessed: Huang Gai of Nanhai became administrator of Rinan; as soon as he arrived, because the reception was not lavish, he clubbed the chief clerk to death and was then driven away.
translations.idiomatic: I myself saw Huang Gai of Nanhai, posted to Rinan, beat his chief clerk to death over a stingy welcome banquet and get chased out by the locals.

sentences.zh: 九真太守儋萌為妻父周京作主人，並請大吏，酒酣作樂。

translations.literal: The administrator of Jiuzhen, Dan Meng, acted as host for his wife’s father Zhou Jing and also invited high officials; when the wine was merry they made music.
translations.idiomatic: Dan Meng of Jiuzhen threw a banquet for his father-in-law Zhou Jing and the senior staff; the wine flowed and musicians played.

sentences.zh: 功曹番歆起舞屬京，京不肯起，歆猶迫強，萌忿杖歆，亡於郡內。

translations.literal: The merit clerk Fan Xin rose to dance and passed the turn to Jing; Jing would not rise, Xin still pressed him forcefully; Meng in anger caned Xin, who died within the commandery.
translations.idiomatic: When the merit clerk Fan Xin tried to pull Zhou Jing into a round dance and Zhou refused, Fan kept badgering him until Governor Dan Meng caned Fan to death on the spot.

sentences.zh: 歆弟苗帥眾攻府，毒矢射萌，萌至物故。

translations.literal: Xin’s younger brother Miao led a host to attack the yamen and shot Meng with poisoned arrows; Meng came to death.
translations.idiomatic: Fan Xin’s brother Fan Miao then stormed the yamen with archers and riddled Dan Meng with poisoned bolts.

sentences.zh: 交阯太守士燮遣兵致討，卒不能克。

translations.literal: The administrator of Jiaozhi, Shi Xie, sent troops to attack and punish them, but in the end could not overcome them.
translations.idiomatic: Shi Xie of Jiaozhi sent troops to punish the mutineers but could not break them.

sentences.zh: 又故刺史會稽朱符，多以鄉人虞褒、劉彥之徒分作長吏，侵虐百姓，強賦於民黃魚一枚收稻一斛，百姓怨叛，山賊並出，攻州突郡。

translations.literal: Moreover the former Inspector Zhu Fu of Kuaiji for the most part appointed his fellow townsmen Yu Bao, Liu Yan, and the like to serve as magistrates, oppressed the common people, and forcibly levied from the people one hu of grain for each yellow fish—until the people bore a grudge and rebelled, mountain bandits arising together and assaulting province and commandery.
translations.idiomatic: Earlier Inspector Zhu Fu of Kuaiji packed the districts with hometown cronies like Yu Bao and Liu Yan, taxed a bushel of rice for every cheap yellow fish, and drove the people into the hills until bandit armies stormed every yamen.

sentences.zh: 符走入海，流離喪亡。

translations.literal: Fu fled into the sea and wandered until he perished.
translations.idiomatic: Zhu Fu fled offshore and died a wanderer.

sentences.zh: 次得南陽張津，與荊州牧劉表為隙，兵弱敵強，歲歲興軍，諸將厭患，去留自在。

translations.literal: Next came Zhang Jin of Nanyang, who had a rift with Governor Liu Biao of Jingzhou; his troops were weak, the enemy strong, and year after year he raised armies until the generals grew weary and resentful, coming and going as they pleased.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Jin of Nanyang feuded with Liu Biao, fielded too few men against too many, and wore his generals out with endless campaigns until they came and went as they pleased.

sentences.zh: 津小檢攝，威武不足，為所陵侮，遂至殺沒。

translations.literal: Jin’s minor restraint and control, insufficient awe-inspiring might, led to his being insulted and bullied until he was killed and lost everything.
translations.idiomatic: Too weak to impose discipline, he was mocked, mutinied against, and finally killed.

sentences.zh: 後得零陵賴恭，先輩仁謹，不曉時事。

translations.literal: After him came Lai Gong of Lingling, an elder generation, benevolent and cautious, ignorant of current affairs.
translations.idiomatic: Lai Gong of Lingling, a kindly elder, understood nothing of realpolitik.

sentences.zh: 表又遣長沙吳巨為蒼梧太守。

translations.literal: Biao also sent Wu Ju of Changsha as administrator of Cangwu.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Biao then sent the brawler Wu Ju from Changsha to govern Cangwu.

sentences.zh: 巨武夫輕悍，不為恭服。

translations.literal: Ju was a brash fighting man, light and fierce, and would not submit to Gong.
translations.idiomatic: Wu Ju was a swaggering soldier who refused to defer to Lai Gong.

sentences.zh: （所取）

translations.literal: (What was taken [lacuna].)
translations.idiomatic: The damaged line here probably recorded the exactions Wu Ju’s officers took from the people.

translations.literal: (At every turn [lacuna].)
translations.idiomatic: A second lacuna likely meant that the two sides clashed again and again.

sentences.zh: 相怨恨，逐出恭，求步騭。

translations.literal: nursed mutual hatred, drove out Gong, and sought Bu Zhi.
translations.idiomatic: They turned on each other in hatred, drove Lai Gong out, and demanded that Bu Zhi be sent to replace him.

sentences.zh: 是時津故將夷廖、錢博之徒尚多，騭以次鋤治，綱紀適定，會仍召出。

translations.literal: At that time many of Jin’s former generals such as Yi Liao and Qian Bo still remained; Bu Zhi eliminated and regulated them in turn until discipline had just been set, when he was again summoned away.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Jin’s old officers—men like Yi Liao and Qian Bo—were still numerous; Bu Zhi uprooted them one by one until order was restored, only to be recalled himself just as the reins tightened.

sentences.zh: 呂岱既至，有士氏之變。

translations.literal: When Lü Dai arrived, there was the mutiny of the Shi clan.
translations.idiomatic: Lü Dai’s arrival coincided with the Shi family’s rebellion in the south.

sentences.zh: 越軍南征，平討之日，改置長吏，章明王綱，威加萬里，大小承風。

translations.literal: When the southern expeditionary force campaigned, on the day pacification was achieved he replaced the senior magistrates, made royal regulation manifest, and extended awe for ten thousand li so that great and small all bent to the wind.
translations.idiomatic: Once the southern armies had pacified the region, the court replaced local strongmen, spelled out imperial law, and projected authority until every rank fell into line.

sentences.zh: 由此言之，綏邊撫裔，實有其人。

translations.literal: Judging from this, for soothing the frontier and cherishing the outer peoples there truly were the right men.
translations.idiomatic: The episode shows that the frontier really did need—and sometimes got—governors equal to the task.

sentences.zh: 牧伯之任，既宜清能，荒流之表，禍福尤甚。

translations.literal: The office of regional shepherd ought to go to the pure and capable; beyond the wasteland margins blessing and disaster weigh all the more heavily.
translations.idiomatic: A border province demands an honest, able hand; out past the wilds, success or ruin weighs twice as heavy.

sentences.zh: 今日交州雖名粗定，尚有高涼宿賊；

translations.literal: Today Jiaozhou, though nominally roughly settled, still harbors entrenched bandits in Gaoliang;
translations.idiomatic: Jiaozhou may look quiet on the map, but Gaoliang still shelters veteran outlaws.

sentences.zh: 其南海、蒼梧、鬱林、珠官四郡界未綏，依作寇盜，專為亡叛逋逃之藪。

translations.literal: Within Nanhai, Cangwu, Yulin, and Zhuguan the four commanderies are not yet pacified; they rely on raiding as a haven for fugitives and rebels.
translations.idiomatic: Nanhai, Cangwu, Yulin, and Zhuguan remain half-tamed—bandit nests that welcome every deserter from the law.

sentences.zh: 若岱不復南，新刺史宜得精密，檢攝八郡，方略智計，能稍稍以漸

translations.literal: If Dai does not return south, the new inspector must be meticulous, able to inspect and bind the eight commanderies, in strategy and wit able little by little by degrees
translations.idiomatic: If Lü Dai stays north, his successor must be a meticulous man who can tighten all eight southern commanderies and advance reform step by step

translations.literal: (to be able)
translations.idiomatic: (the lacuna likely read “to be able” to complete the previous clause)

sentences.zh: 治高涼者，假其威寵，借之形勢，責其成效，庶幾可補復。

translations.literal: —one who governs Gaoliang ought to lend him prestige and authority, borrow him circumstance, and demand visible results—then perhaps restoration may be possible.
translations.idiomatic: —whoever pacifies Gaoliang must be backed with real rank, given leverage, and held to results if the south is ever to heal.

sentences.zh: 如但中人。

translations.literal: If he is only middling,
translations.idiomatic: If you send merely average talent,

sentences.zh: 近守常法，無奇數異術者，則群惡日滋，久遠成害。

translations.literal: clinging near to ordinary law without unusual stratagems, then evils will daily increase and in time become lasting harm.
translations.idiomatic: someone who enforces the letter of routine statutes without imagination will let corruption spread until it becomes a chronic plague.

sentences.zh: 故國之安危，在於所任，不可不察也。

translations.literal: Therefore the state’s safety or peril lies in whom you appoint; it cannot but be examined.
translations.idiomatic: The realm’s fate rides on these appointments; the choice deserves the closest scrutiny.

sentences.zh: 竊懼朝廷忽輕其選，故敢竭愚情，以廣聖思。

translations.literal: I privately fear the court may lightly neglect this selection; therefore I dare exhaust my foolish sincerity to broaden sagely deliberation.
translations.idiomatic: I fear the capital may treat the posting as routine; I therefore presume to speak plainly in hope of widening Your Majesty’s counsel.

sentences.zh: 黃龍三年，建昌侯慮為鎮軍大將軍，屯半州，以綜為長史，外掌眾事，內授書籍。

translations.literal: In the third year of Huanglong, when Marquis of Jianchang Lü was General Who Guards the Army stationed at Banzhou, Zong was made his chief clerk, outwardly managing the host of affairs and inwardly presenting books and documents.
translations.idiomatic: In Huanglong 3 Sun Lü, marquis of Jianchang, camped at Banzhou as general who guards the army and took Xue Zong as chief clerk—Zong ran day-to-day business abroad and tutored him with texts at home.

sentences.zh: 慮卒，入守賊曹尚書，遷尚書僕射。

translations.literal: When Lü died, Zong entered as Supervisor of Public Bandits in the Masters of Writing, then was promoted Vice Director.
translations.idiomatic: After Sun Lü died, Xue Zong entered the secretariat as supervisor of public bandits and soon rose to vice director.

sentences.zh: 時公孫淵降而復叛，權盛怒，欲自親征。

translations.literal: When Gongsun Yuan submitted then rebelled again, Quan was greatly enraged and wished to lead a campaign in person.
translations.idiomatic: Gongsun Yuan’s renewed defection so enraged Sun Quan that he meant to take the field himself.

sentences.zh: 綜上疏諫曰：

translations.literal: Zong submitted a memorial remonstrating, saying:
translations.idiomatic: Xue Zong answered with a long memorial that opened:

sentences.zh: 夫帝王者，萬國之元首，天下之所繫命也。

translations.literal: The emperor-king is the head of the myriad states; on him the world hangs its life.
translations.idiomatic: The Son of Heaven is the pivot of every kingdom; all lives depend on his person.

sentences.zh: 是以居則重門擊柝以戒不虞，行則清道案節以養威嚴，蓋所以存萬安之福，鎮四海之心。

translations.literal: Therefore at rest he layers gates and strikes the clapper to guard against the unforeseen; on the march he clears the road and curbs the pace to nurture awe and majesty—thereby preserving the blessing of perfect security and steadying the heart within the four seas.
translations.idiomatic: At court he multiplies gates and night watches; on campaign he clears roads and slows the train—all to keep catastrophe at bay and reassure the realm.

sentences.zh: 昔孔子疾時，托乘桴浮海之語，季由斯喜，拒以無所取才。

translations.literal: Formerly Confucius, sick of his age, lodged the words of “riding a raft out to sea”; Zilu then rejoiced, and was refused on the ground that he had no talent worth taking.
translations.idiomatic: Confucius once spoke bitterly of sailing away on a raft; Zilu brightened at the thought, only to be told he was not the man for such an errand.

sentences.zh: 漢元帝欲禦樓船，薛廣德請刎頸以血染車。

translations.literal: When Emperor Yuan of Han wished to board the tower-ship, Xue Guangde begged to cut his throat and dye the chariot with his blood.
translations.idiomatic: When Han Yuandi wanted to ride the war-barges, Xue Guangde offered to slit his own throat to stop the chariot wheels.

sentences.zh: 何則？

translations.literal: Why?
translations.idiomatic: Why?

sentences.zh: 水火之險至危，非帝王所宜涉也。

translations.literal: The peril of water and fire is supremely dangerous—it is not what a ruler should brave.
translations.idiomatic: Wind and waves are the deadliest odds a sovereign can face.

sentences.zh: 諺曰：『千金之子，坐不垂堂。

translations.literal: The proverb says: “The heir to a thousand in gold does not sit beneath the high hall’s eaves.”
translations.idiomatic: The proverb runs, “A prince’s son does not lounge under a risky cornice.”

sentences.zh: 』況萬乘之尊乎？

translations.literal: How much more the honor of ten thousand chariots?
translations.idiomatic: How much truer for the rider of ten thousand chariots?

sentences.zh: 今遼東戎貊小國，無城池之固，備御之術，器械銖鈍，犬羊無政，往必禽克，誠如明詔。

translations.literal: Now Liaodong is a Rong-Mo petty state without firm walls or arts of defense; its weapons are blunt as scrap iron; it is like dogs and sheep without governance—were you to go you would certainly seize them, just as the enlightened edict declares.
translations.idiomatic: Liaodong is a barbarian backwater—no walls, no drill, arms that would not cut butter, command like a flock without a shepherd. Your edict is right: a strike would crush them.

sentences.zh: 然其方土寒埆，谷稼不殖，民習鞍馬，轉徙無常。

translations.literal: Yet its soil is cold and barren, grain will not grow there, the people are used to saddled horses and shift dwelling without constancy.
translations.idiomatic: Yet the ground is poor, crops fail, and the people live in the saddle, drifting wherever pasture leads.

sentences.zh: 卒聞大軍之至，自度不敵，鳥驚獸駭，長驅奔竄，一人匹馬，不可得見。

translations.literal: If on a sudden they hear a great army has come, they will reckon themselves unequal, scatter like startled birds and beasts in long flight—with one man on one horse you may not catch sight of one.
translations.idiomatic: Word of a host marching north will send them flying before you can fix a battle line—you may win only empty steppe.

sentences.zh: 雖獲空地，守之無益，此不可一也；

translations.literal: Though you gain empty land, guarding it brings no benefit—this is the first thing that will not do;
translations.idiomatic: Empty grassland is the first reason the venture is hollow;

sentences.zh: 加又洪流滉瀁，有成山之難，海行無常，風波難免，倏忽之間，人船異勢。

translations.literal: further the great billows surge wide and deep, with the peril of Chengshan; sea travel is inconstant, wind and wave cannot be avoided—between blinks men and ships may meet different fates.
translations.idiomatic: second, the ocean between you and them is a wall of storms like Cape Chengshan—ships vanish in a squall’s blink;

sentences.zh: 雖有堯、舜之德，智無所施，賁、育之勇，力不得設，此不可二也；

translations.literal: though one had the virtue of Yao and Shun, wisdom would have nowhere to apply; though one had the courage of Meng Ben and Xia Yu, strength would have nowhere to deploy—this is the second thing that will not do;
translations.idiomatic: second, even Yao and Shun could not govern a deck in a typhoon, nor could Meng Ben’s brawn trim a sail—

sentences.zh: 加以鬱霧冥其上，鹹水蒸其下，生流腫，轉相洿染，凡行海者，稀無斯患，此不可三也。

translations.literal: add fog brooding above and brine steaming below, sores and swellings forming, contagion spreading one to another—scarcely any who sail the sea lack this affliction; this is the third thing that will not do.
translations.idiomatic: third, fog, brine, ship fever, and plague ship to ship—no fleet escapes the southern sea unscathed.

sentences.zh: 天生神聖，顯以符瑞，當乘平喪亂，康此民物；

translations.literal: Heaven bore the sacred sage to display omens and signs so that you should ride calm and end chaos, bringing peace to this people;
translations.idiomatic: Heaven marked you as sage to end turmoil and heal the folk;

sentences.zh: 嘉祥日集，海內垂定，逆虜凶虐，滅亡在近。

translations.literal: auspicious omens gather daily, within the seas peace is nearly settled, the cruel traitor’s violence approaches extinction.
translations.idiomatic: good omens pile up at home while the traitor in the north withers;

sentences.zh: 中國一平，遼東自斃，但當拱手以待耳。

translations.literal: once the Central States are pacified Liaodong will die of itself—you need only fold your hands and wait.
translations.idiomatic: pacify the heartland and Liaodong falls without a spear cast—only fold your hands and wait.

sentences.zh: 今乃違必然之圖，尋至危之阻，忽九州之固，，肆一朝之忿，既非社稷之重計，又開闢以來所未嘗有，斯誠群僚所以傾身側息，食不甘味，寢不安席者也。

translations.literal: Now to abandon a plan that is certain, seek out the most perilous obstacles, neglect the security of the Nine Provinces, indulge a morning’s wrath—this is neither a weighty scheme for the altars of soil and grain, nor has it been seen since the world was opened—this is truly why your ministers bend their bodies and hold their breath, find food tasteless, and cannot rest on their mats.
translations.idiomatic: Yet now you would spurn the sure path, brave the deadliest straits, shrug off the empire’s inner defenses, and vent a morning’s temper—a gamble the altars have never seen and one that keeps every minister sleepless and sick at heart.

sentences.zh: 惟陛下抑雷霆之威，忍赫斯之怒，遵乘橋之安，遠履冰之險，則臣子賴祉，天下幸甚。

translations.literal: Only may Your Majesty check the thunderbolt might, restrain the sovereign wrath, follow the safety of riding the bridge, shun the peril of treading on ice—then your servants will receive blessing and the realm will be greatly fortunate.
translations.idiomatic: Check the thunder of your anger, choose the firm bridge over thin ice, and your servants will live secure—the realm will count itself blessed.

sentences.zh: 時群臣多諫，權遂不行。

translations.literal: At that time many of the ministers remonstrated, and Quan thereupon did not go.
translations.idiomatic: The court chorus joined Xue Zong’s plea, and Sun Quan gave up the expedition.

sentences.zh: 正月乙未，權敕綜祝祖不得用常文，綜承詔，卒造文義，信辭粲爛。

translations.literal: On yichou day of the first month Quan ordered Zong that the prayer to the ancestor must not use common phrasing; Zong received the edict and on the spot composed text whose meaning and rhetoric blazed bright.
translations.idiomatic: On the yichou day of the first month Sun Quan told Xue Zong to avoid stock phrases in the ancestral prayer; Zong improvised lines so brilliant that the court murmured approval.

sentences.zh: 權曰：「復為兩頭。

translations.literal: Quan said: “Again make a two-headed one.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor said, “Give me another couplet—two heads.”

sentences.zh: 使滿三也。

translations.literal: Let it reach three.”
translations.idiomatic: “And stretch the whole thing to three.”

sentences.zh: 」綜復再祝，辭令皆新，眾咸稱善。

translations.literal: Zong prayed twice more; the wording was all new, and the crowd praised it.
translations.idiomatic: Zong offered two more prayers in fresh language, and everyone praised him.

sentences.zh: 赤烏三年，徙選曹尚書。

translations.literal: In the third year of Chiwu he was transferred to be Director of Personnel.
translations.idiomatic: In Chiwu 3 he moved to head the bureau of appointments.

sentences.zh: 五年，為太子少傅，領選職如故。

translations.literal: In the fifth year he became Junior Tutor to the Heir, still holding his selection duties as before.
translations.idiomatic: Two years later he became junior tutor to the crown prince while keeping his personnel portfolio.

sentences.zh: 〈吳書曰：後權賜綜紫綬囊，綜陳讓紫色非所宜服，權曰：「太子年少，涉道日淺，君當博之以文，約之以禮，茅土之封，非君而誰？

translations.literal: The Book of Wu states: Later Quan gave Zong a purple-silk ribbon purse; Zong declined, saying purple was not what he should wear. Quan said: “The heir is still young, shallow in the Way day by day; you should broaden him with letters and bind him with ritual—if not you, who deserves the fief with hallowed soil?”
translations.idiomatic: The Wu chronicle adds that when Sun Quan gave him a purple ribbon bag Xue Zong demurred as over-ranked; Quan answered that the young heir needed a scholar of his stature to teach letters and ritual—“who else should wear the colors of high enfeoffment?”

sentences.zh: 」是時綜以名儒居師傅之位，仍兼選舉，甚為優重。〉

translations.literal: At this time Zong, as a famed scholar, occupied the tutor’s seat while still holding appointments—very honored.〉
translations.idiomatic: Thus Xue Zong stood as the heir’s preceptor and chief talent scout—an office doubly honored.〉

sentences.zh: 六年春，卒。

translations.literal: In the spring of the sixth year he died.
translations.idiomatic: He died in the spring of the sixth year of that reign.

sentences.zh: 凡所著詩賦難論數萬言，名曰《私載》，又定《五宗圖述》、《二京解》，皆傳於世。

translations.literal: In all he composed odes, fu, and disquisitions numbering tens of thousands of graphs, collected under the title Private Collation, and also fixed the Five Clans Chart and Discourse and Explaining the Two Capitals—all of which passed down in the world.
translations.idiomatic: His literary remains—odes, rhapsodies, and essays gathered as *Private Collation*, plus his *Five Clans Chart* and *Explaining the Two Capitals*—ran to tens of thousands of characters and stayed in circulation.

sentences.zh: 子珝，官至威南將軍，徵交阯還，道病死。

translations.literal: His son Xu rose to General Who Awes the South; returning from the expedition against Jiaozhi he died of illness on the road.
translations.idiomatic: His son Xue Xu became general who awes the south but took sick and died on the march home from Jiaozhi.

sentences.zh: 〈《漢晉春秋》曰：孫休時，珝為五宮中郎將，遣至蜀求馬。

translations.literal: The Han-Jin chunqiu states: Under Sun Xiu, Xu was Colonel of the Gentlemen of the Household of the Five Palaces, sent to Shu to seek horses.
translations.idiomatic: The *Han-Jin chunqiu* notes that under Sun Xiu, Xue Xu served as colonel of the household gentlemen of the five palaces and rode to Shu to buy horses.

sentences.zh: 及還，休問蜀政得失，對曰：「主闇而不知其過，臣下容身以求免罪，入其朝不聞正言，經其野民皆菜色。

translations.literal: When he returned, Xiu asked him about the gains and losses of Shu’s government; he answered: “The ruler is dim yet knows no fault; ministers keep their persons to escape guilt; entering their court one hears no straight words; passing their fields the people all wear the look of famine.”
